subsubtopic: ALLEGED DIRECTIVE THAT LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS BE GRANTED WHEN ORDERED BY APPEAL BOARD-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity arising from a telex directive sent by the director of immigration for the Ontario region to all officers in charge of Canada immigration centres and subsequently circulated under date of October 15, 1975 by E. J. Fanning of the Canada Immigration Centre in Toronto to immigration supervisors. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington):
That the Minister of Manpower and Immigration make a statement concerning recent instructions under which immigration officers at Canada immigration centres now operate, which state that immediate landed immigrant status is to be granted any person where such is ordered by the Immigration Appeal Board regardless of whether immigration officials have received necessary medical examination reports, or whether immigration officials have completed investigations required regarding criminal or subversive backgrounds which would be harmful to national security, and further that the minister forthwith assure the House that steps will be taken to prevent the Immigration Appeal Board from hearing future cases without availability of all evidence at the time, that the minister guarantee immediate legislative steps will be taken to prevent continuance of a situation whereby criminals, subversives and other undesirables can receive landed immigrant status by Immigration Appeal Board decisions, and finally that the minister make public the number of such individuals to date receiving landed immigrant status in this way.

subtopic: U410)   THE CANADIAN ECONOMY ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-LENGTH OF PROVINCIAL COMMITMENT TO GUIDELINES ACCEPTABLE TO GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance.
I should like to ask the minister whether the government is still asking the provinces to enter into an agreement with the Government of Canada for a full three or three and a quarter years, the full term of the government's anti-inflationary program, or whether the government has indicated that it is prepared to accept a shorter commitment from the provinces. I am thinking particularly of those provinces deciding to let the federal government administer the plan with regard to their own civil servants, and so forth.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with regard to the public sector, which is the part which is being discussed with the provinces, we discussed at the most recent meeting the notion of entering in for a period shorter than the full period of the program with the expectation that there would be a review and a renewal at the end of that shorter period.

speechtext: that is the appropriate technique with respect to the provinces, I wonder why the minister could not have agreed to it with respect to the program generally, as we suggested. However, I should like to ask the minister how he reconciles accepting the shorter commitment with the provinces-I heard the term a year and a half mentioned-with the government's whole concept of a program of gradually phasing down inflation over a period of three or three and a quarter years.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-RECONCILIATION OF ACCEPTANCE OF SHORTER COMMITMENT FROM PROVINCES WITH LONGER PROGRAM OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Our
distinct preference was to phase inflation down more slowly over the three year period rather than have a very sharp reduction, which would bring about certain risks in the way of unemployment. Our distinct preference is to go on that slower incline. On the other hand, we have recognized that the provinces are sovereign governments in Canada, and that the best means of achieving this is with their agreement. We hoped to get their agreement to the longer period. If their agreement can only be obtained by their entering into an initially shorter period with the hope of renewal, that is the second best, but that is still a preferable solution to having no provincial participation in the public sector at all.

speechtext:

Would the Minister of External Affairs advise what his progress is on the abduction cases of (a) Mrs. Stephanie Gribbon, Surrey, British Columbia, one child abducted and taken to Portugal in 1973 (b) Mrs. Jean Hobbs, Victoria, British Columbia, three children abducted and taken to the United States in 1972 (c) Mrs. Nicolette, Vancouver, British Columbia, three children abducted and taken to Italy in 1973 (d) Mrs. Mildred Clarke, Mission, British Columbia, five children abducted and taken to the Philippines in 1974?

speechtext:

(a) In the case of Mrs. Gribben, in response to a request by the British Columbia authorities that the father be extradited from Portugal to face abduction charges in Canada, the Department obtained a legal opinion from Portugal that extradition was not possible in the circumstances and that Mrs. Gribben must seek a custody order in the Court of Minors in Portugal. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, back on May 21, 1975, I first had the opportunity to make some brief remarks respecting my position on Bill C-20. At that time I pointed out quite clearly that the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons was conducting hearings across Canada relative to future or possible changes in Canada's immigration laws, and that the question of citizenship and its requirements were part and parcel of that discussion. It was my view at that time that the debate should be delayed until such time as the committee had had an opportunity to present to the House the findings it was able to make in its travels across Canada and at hearings in Ottawa. With your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, I intend to bring to your attention and to the attention of the House some of the recommendations of that committee as they reflect on Canada's present citizenship act.
Also in my brief remarks on May 21 I stressed the positive aspects of the bill, namely, that the bill will correct a deficiency which now exists in the Canadian Citizenship Act in that it is proposed that citizenship be granted to a child born outside of Canada if one of his or her parents is a Canadian citizen. It is a right that is presently only held by male members of our society but which should be extended to female members. That provision in the bill has my endorsation.
The second matter concerns lowering the eligibility age from 21 to 18. It stated on May 21 that those regulations should have been brought in when the Canada Elections Act was amended. That is another deficiency which Bill C-20 corrects. The central thrust of Bill C-20, as I see it, is the reduction of the waiting period for residency requirements and qualifications of landed immigrants, which at the present time is five years; that is, five years from the time an immigrant receives landed immigrant status when he can apply for citizenship and become a Canadian citizen if he fulfils the requirements.
The proponents of this provision argue that five years is an arbitrary figure and say that three years is more equitable. They say, also, that it reduces somewhat the arbitrariness of the act and the stigma of having to wait a long period of time which could make immigrants feel they are regarded as second-class citizens. I pointed out on May 21 that the residency requirements presently in effect in the United States, Britain, Belgium, West Germany, Australia and New Zealand are generally five years or longer. I am sure hon. members could also point to the fact that in some countries the residency requirements are less than five years, and that this period of time would be no less or no more arbitrary than the present requirement of five years in Canada.
However, I should like to point out that very few countries in the world could be termed receiving countries, that is, countries which receive significant numbers of immigrants yearly. Canada happens to be one of these countries. There are very few countries in the world which meet those qualifications. In fact, in the last five years Canada has welcomed to its shores approximately one million immigrants. So I suggest that our citizenship requirements have slightly different ramifications from those of countries which have very few people coming in as landed immigrants.
(Mr. MacEachen.]
December 8, 1975

All of us should ask ourselves whether we have given immigrants an adequate opportunity to adapt to the Canadian way of life. During the hearings of the joint committee the question of adaptation received a fair amount of attention and discussion. We found, for example, that generally speaking-I know we have to generalize in circumstances such as these-studies show that immigrants have an income equal to or higher than the average income of native born Canadians shortly after they come to Canada. So the economic adjustment that immigrants make is relatively quick and generally painless, and the positive factors are there not only for the immigrants but for Canada as a whole.
On the matter of language, it was found that despite the horrendous problems they were exposed to in places like the Toronto school system-if my memory serves me correctly, at one Toronto school there were about 18 mother tongues represented in one elementary classroom-and despite what one might call the pedagogical problems that situation represents, generally children of immigrants adapted to either one or both of the official languages of Canada in relatively short order.
The government must keep in mind that much more has to be done at the tripartite level. The federal government must assume more responsibility, in my view, and when immigrants come into Canada they should not then say to the provinces and municipalities, "Here they are. You are responsible": the federal government has to go beyond that. I am sure all hon. members recognize that the residency qualifications are really for one purpose, and that is for the immigrant to be able to adapt to the Canadian way of life upon which is based his citizenship. At least to some degree adaptation has to be made.
It was also very clear that we were not very successful in having immigrant women adapt to the Canadian way of life and become part of the social milieu. This was quite clearly pointed out in the immigration brief. I should like to read a portion of it into the record. I am reading from page 53:41 of the report of the Special Joint Committee on Immigration Policy as follows:
Attention was also directed to the particular plight of immigrant women, and especially wives and mothers. When they are not in the work force they have little opportunity to learn the language and make personal contacts, advantages enjoyed by their husbands and their school-aged and working children. Many of them remain in the home isolated by language differences, and can become estranged from the community and even from their own families.
It was pointed out that language training is the single most important need of these women. The committee is aware that federal funds are made available to the provinces to finance courses organized through the adult education division of the schools. But committee members gained the impression that not enough attention has been paid to this program by the responsible authorities and recommends that it be reviewed.
I think the evidence is quite clear that whether it be five years, three years or whatever, we are not doing enough to give members of the immigrant community an opportunity to adapt to the Canadian way of life, specifically with regard to language to which I have already referred. If people come to Canada and take Canada as the country of which they want to become citizens, we must ask ourselves what is the proper waiting time. I fully admit that whether
Citizenship
it be five years or three years, it cannot be argued as an arbitrary time. I recognize that. I think we must consider what we are going to do in the three-year period or the five-year period, whatever the case may be, to make immigrants who are potential citizens feel at home and encourage them to make the contribution of which they are capable.
So often in our society we stress rights; we stress also the rights of immigrants, for instance, when they are being interviewed in the country of which they are citizens. When they come to Canada we also point out their rights. I believe we should stress more the obligations in a democratic society. Not only does this apply to immigrants but also to native born Canadians. I think there has been a glaring deficiency in that part of our educational program. We have not given enough thought, direction and thrust to the training of immigrants and our young people as to the obligations a democracy imposes.
I would like to point out that by the teaching of obligations we will not create negative reactions; I feel that this would do just the opposite. In order to create in our immigrants and our young people a love for Canada, regardless of the period of time we are considering, the minister, the government and Canadians generally should consider this matter seriously and work out a citizenship training period and citizenship courses which will create for all of us a commonalty as to what we think Canadian citizenship means and what its rights and obligations are.
I should like to point out that at the present time we are receiving a number of immigrants who come from countries which do not have strong democratic traditions. It would be for the benefit not only of Canadians but also of immigrants if we taught them not only language, economic adjustment and social adjustment, but also their obligations in their new country. For too long our public schools and citizenship courses have been lacking in this area. I am not preaching an extreme nationalism. I know that for many years Canadians have almost recoiled at the thought that we should try and push nationalism. I am not looking at this matter in terms of negative nationalism or blind allegiance but, rather, as something which should be done in a positive manner.
As we consider Bill C-20 I must be very frank and say that I have certain views on the five-year limit, but when I consider the statistics with regard to people who came before the committee, who wrote to the committee in letter form or prepared a brief, I find that Canadians are rather inconclusive as to whether it should be made five years or reduced to something less or, as the bill suggests, to three years. In respect of that issue I should like to read into the record how the committee thought Canadians generally viewed citizenship requirements and changes which might be possible. I read from page 53:49, paragraph 12 of the same report:
Most persons expressing these concerns felt that government has lost control of the immigration flow. Submissions revealed a lack of public confidence in the ability of government to manage the size of immigration movements, the racial and ethnic composition of the Canadian population, and the settlement of newcomers in underpopulated regions and away from the large cities. The ability of Canadian communities to absorb newcomers, and the role of government in aiding immigrants in their initial settlement and integration, were also primary concerns.

December 8, 1975
Citizenship
Many people in Canada, as they viewed our immigration laws, made one point time after time. I do not have time to go into the statistics, but the point they stressed was that the reaction to immigration today-many briefs pointed this out-was largely spawned or largely due to the fact that people felt in many areas the government had lost, so to speak, the handle or control of immigration flows. For that purpose I should like to read from page 53:42 of the same report:
Many submissions received by the committee suggested that if Canada's record of successful multicultural adaptation is to be maintained, more attention must be given to the development of programs related to cross-cultural and inter-racial understanding . .. Should an assessment show a need for significantly expanded national, community and school programs to promote intercultural harmony, the committee believes-

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) has the floor. If other hon. members have anything to say, I wish they would wait.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
I will repeat:
Should an assessment show a need for significantly expanded national, community and school programs to promote intercultural harmony, the committee believes the federal government should explore with the provinces ways of encouraging and implementing such programs.
I believe we will only have to teach immigrant Canadians that this is a bilingual, bicultural country, but also that it is a multicultural country. These should not be empty words, either. The program should not be constantly threatened by cutbacks or, as is presently the case, by extinction. All we have to do in this regard is look at the testimony of the Canadian consultative committee which has said that the Minister of Labour who is responsible for multiculturalism has virtually abandoned his portfolio. Rather, we should look upon multiculturalism, and the contributions these Canadians can make, as a positive force.
I look forward to the committee hearings when the minister and his officials can outline the advantages of reducing the period of residency qualification from five years to three. If this is the time that is necessary for immigrants to adapt socially, economically and culturally, I should like to see it demonstrated and know what programs the minister has in mind to encourage the use of immigrant talents and abilities. One part of the bill which I cannot support in any way is clause 5 on page 4. I should like to read it into the record:
5. (1) The minister shall grant citizenship to any person who, not being a citizen makes application therefor and
Then follow the paragraph:
(b) (i) for every day during which he was resident in Canada before his lawful admission to Canada for permanent residence he shall be deemed to have accumulated one-half of a day of residence-
The way I understand that provision is this: it means that an alien-let us not even say "illegal immigrant", because I do not believe you can use the two words in the same context-who is here illegally for six years, under the terms of that clause can be given citizenship on the ground

that he has fulfilled three years of the residency requirement. For every two days in Canada, one day is counted toward his residency qualification, so I read it the minister is saying that parliament will now make legal what to date has been illegal. This is preposterous, Mr. Speaker. I wish the minister could give us an assurance that this clause will be deleted from the bill. It certainly would improve it. I say that because I do not want to make legal something which is illegal.
All around the country immigration officers at private talks stressed time and time again that they needed manpower and sophisticated investigative devices to cope with the large, international movement of illegals. They stressed that the type of illegal they come in contact with often has international connections, sometimes criminal, particularly with drug trafficking on an international scale. They asked for the tools to do a good job either at the primary inspection line or the secondary inspection line.
The immigration program in the last few years has suffered because in the minds of Canadians the alien who enters Canada illegally has been equated with those who came legally and wanted to make a contribution to the country. As the clause stands, it gives the appearance that the minister is in favour of legalizing something that is presently illegal, and it forces members of the House to condone something that is wrong. It also erodes the confidence that we should have in our immigration officers and RCMP special officers who are concerned with these movements every day. For the life of me I cannot find any purpose in this clause.
In his speech, the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) did not say why he felt clause 5 was necessary. We hear all kinds of estimates of the number of illegals in the United States and Canada, but I am sure no one knows exactly what the figures are. Canada is attractive and people want to make a home here, so it is natural that a number come this way. But surely the minister does not wish to see a clause in the bill which will erode the work presently being done by his officials. If he knows of some good reason why this clause should be included, I should like to hear it, but I think the bill would be enhanced if it were amended.
Another clause that I should like to deal with concerns the hearing before a judge of the citizenship court. The judge has no right to defer the application. Sometimes the judge may feel that the applicant is not ready for citizenship and that a review in six months' time would be in order. If the bill is passed as it stands, however, the judge must hear the case and within 60 days he must make a decision. If the application is denied, the applicant is informed of his right of appeal, and once that process is carried out that is the end of it. I feel that if a judge considers that a delay of six months or a year will help the person adjust to Canadian life, a delay should be granted.
Bill C-20 makes many positive contributions, but we must ask ourselves, first, if the change from five years to three years will ensure that people have truly become Canadians, are proud of Canadian life and will make a contribution to Canada. We must also ask if a person who has been in Canada illegally should be allowed to use 50 per cent of that time to go toward the residency qualification. I look forward to the committee hearings, Mr. Speak-
December 8, 1975

er, and I hope the minister can give us some positive reasons why the bill should be accepted by members of this House.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 21 last the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) gave this party's view of Bill C-20, saying that in general we approve of the changes embodied in it and we propose to support it on second reading. There are one or two observations that I should like to make, however. One of the reasons we approve of the bill is that it represents a step forward in establishing equal rights for women. In many respects the previous act was discriminatory. Under it, a person born outside Canada who had been lawfully admitted to this country and whose father or, in the case of a person born out of wedlock, whose mother was born in Canada was considered a natural born Canadian citizen.
Under the new act a person born outside Canada will be a Canadian citizen if either of his parents were Canadian citizens. There is no distinction between men and women in this respect. Under the old act there was provision for a father to apply for citizenship for a minor child, or for a mother to do it in the case of an illegitimate child. Under the new act each parent will have an equal right to apply.
Further, under the new act spouses will be treated equally when they apply for Canadian citizenship. That is to say, both men and women when applying will need to be 18 years of age or older and to have lived in Canada for at least three years. Under the old act the spouse of a Canadian citizen who had resided in Canada was entitled to apply for citizenship, I think after one year. Under section 10 of the new act any woman who has lost her citizenship by reason of marriage or the acquisition by her husband of foreign nationality may require citizenship by giving the minister notice in writing that she elects to be a citizen. There appears to be no such provisions in the old act.
Incidentally, at least two of the bill's provisions owe their existence to private members' bills put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He, in turn, secured the ideas for these amendments from someone to whom I wish to pay tribute, Grace Maclnnis, formerly a member of this House. My party has a long history of supporting equality for women, particularly in the important field of citizenship. One of the basic changes in the new act is that the age for application for citizenship is reduced from 21 years to 18 years. Most of us think that is a good idea. We grant citizens the right to vote at age 18 and there is no reason why non-citizens who otherwise qualify should wait until they are 21 before they can apply for citizenship.
I have already, by implication, referred to the reduction to three years of residence in Canada as a necessary qualification for citizenship. In the original act, five years residence was the qualification. In our view, three years residence in Canada is enough to determine if an applicant has adequate knowledge of Canada, of the responsibilities and privileges of citizens and of one of the official languages. These are still requisites or, at least, alternative requirements, for the granting of citizenship. If a person in a period of three years can satisfy the citizenship court, that should be enough. The ability to become established in
Citizenship
Canada can surely be determined within a three-year period. Indeed, evidence and experience show that although most new immigrants may experience initial difficulties in adjusting to Canadian life, they can and do adjust very well within three years.
I am glad to note that the minister's power and discretion have on the whole been considerably reduced. Under section 10 of the old act it is provided that the minister may, in his discretion, grant a certificate of citizenship, etc. The bill now being debated provides that the minister shall grant citizenship and the matter is then referred to the citizenship court. This is a step away from arbitrary ministerial discretion to a judicial decision. I am sure the minister will be glad to have this burden taken off his shoulders.
I regret one thing: by virtue of section 18, the act continues to preserve an unfettered power to the governor in council to intervene and prevent any judicial hearing or appeal in a case in which the governor in council declares that the grant of citizenship would be prejudicial to the security of Canada or contrary to public order in Canada. I am not clear what the last phrase means. It is made clear that the exercise of this power is put beyond review by the citizenship court or, indeed, any other court. The declaration by the governor in council is stated to be conclusive.
It has been my experience that the worst cases of denial of citizenship fall within the category in which security reasons are put forward as grounds for refusing the grant of citizenship. In the past, at least, these so-called security reasons were sometimes based upon the failure of the police to distinguish between radical or left-wing opinions on the one hand and danger to the security of the state on the other. Sometimes they were even based on cases of mistaken identity. I do not believe that this power should be exercised without provision for appeal or any sort of review.
I appreciate that it has often been said that such absolute and arbitrary powers are required because security demands that the sources of information should not be disclosed. There is a way round this, as we discovered during the Second World War when many people of German, Italian and Japanese origin were interned, without reason given, on so-called security grounds. But the regulations were amended to provide for a tribunal composed of a judge of superior or county court rank to review these detention orders. No one was required to disclose publicly the sources of the information on which the detention was based. Some particulars were required to be given to the person detained by order in council. I never heard it suggested that this quasi-judicial type of hearing interfered in any way with the security and safety of the state.
On the other hand, many who were detained were ordered to be released and injustices due, no doubt, to overreaction and overzealous action on the part of those responsible for the internment were righted. Those people were released. I never heard of any harm coming from this process. Indeed, it represented an extension of justice and freedom in wartime when we were very sensitive about questions involving security. If that could be done in wartime, I see no reason for not doing it in peacetime. I suggest that those denied citizenship should be given the right to that sort of quasi-judicial inquiry. Sources of
9806

Citizenship
information could be kept secret. I suggest that we need some form of review to be undertaken by a judicial authority.
I am interested and pleased to note that the requirements for citizenship do not include the provision of the old act, that the applicant must be of good character. Instead, there seems to be substituted the necessity of showing an adequate knowledge of Canada, of the responsibilities and privileges of citizenship, and a "substantial knowledge of Canada." This is an improvement. Obviously, it is difficult to judge the good or bad character of would-be citizens, just as it is difficult to divide native born Canadians into sheep and goats. That must be left to a higher judgment. Yet the requirement for some knowledge of Canada and the privileges of citizenship is useful and reasonable. It is too bad it cannot be made retroactive and applied to all native born Canadians or to those who have the privilege of being citizens. However, I am comforted by the alternative provided, namely, a substantial connection with Canada. I find it unclear whether an adequate knowledge of Canada or of the responsibilities and privileges of citizenship is an alternative to the knowledge of languages. The clause as drafted appears in legal terms to be disjunctive, in other words, to make these alternatives.
One thing interests me. I see reference to the official status of a citizen of the Commonwealth provided for. The minister is not here at the moment. I do not know why not; he should be here. I would like to ask him some time, when he does deign to be present when his legislation is being considered, what is the significance, if any, of being a citizenship of the Commonwealth in Canada. Is this just a word, or does it mean something in actual status? However, taken all in all, this bill deserves our support, certainly at this second reading stage.
Canadian citizenship is of great importance. It is an essential element in our democratic system. It is a matter of special pride to those who have made their homes and plan to live their lives in Canada and are anxious to assume the responsibilities of full citizenship and exercise the full privileges of that status. It is important, therefore, that anomalies, arbitrary provisions and unnecessary obstructions to citizenship be removed. That is the direction of this bill and that is why we support it at this stage.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) for his analysis of the bill. He approached it in a manner that attempted to dissect the meaning behind some clauses contained in the bill that could in future be a possible source of surprise. It might be worthwhile to devote a couple of minutes to a brief explanation of the motives that lie behind the decision of a person to apply for Canadian citizenship. It may not be necessary for most members of this House, but it might be helpful to some on the other side who seem to waiver, as did the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), between the merits of the three-year residential requirement as opposed to the five-year requirement.
The moment a person decides to leave, cross the ocean and come to Canada, he has made a major decision. It means severing friendships, bonds and roots in the country
of origin in order to emigrate to a far away land called Canada. The making of that decision is the beginning of a commitment of certain importance. The person arrives in Canada. He is struck by a variety of feelings and sensations, such as a great sense of space, freedom of movement, mobility and, of course, a great sense of opportunity is grasped by that person, depending upon his or her abilities. That experience upon arrival usually further cements the process of eventual full attachment to this country through the conventional process called acquiring Canadian citizenship.
I am sure some members of this House will share the view that becoming a Canadian citizen is a process which begins many years before in the life of such a person. It is finalized at a certain point of life in Canada when the immigrant comes to the conclusion that this is exactly what he wants to do about his future as a citizen of this country. Against this background, the decision in the homeland, the emotional experience upon arrival and in the years following, and the development of a profound attachment to and fondness for a country in which one did not happen to be born but has conscientiously chosen, the number of years to which the hon. member for Provencher attached so much importance becomes almost irrelevant. It is arbitrary whether it is five or three years.
This bill provides an open door for those who after three years are ready to become members of the Canadian family. In other words, for those who are ready, they can take this step relatively early in their phase of adjustment in Canada. They can simply come forward without having to wait five years. It could be after one, two, three or four years. We could debate this matter for a long time. The fact remains that you provide for a number of years that seems to be reasonably short for those who are ready, early, to take the step. As an example, I would refer to the Czechoslovakian refugees who came here in 1968. They asked for Canadian citizenship on the day they had been here five years. I suspect they would have done the same after three years, or four years. They were ready. They knew it. This was their future. This was their country. They came forward and asked for the Canadian citizenship. I really do not know what else can be said about this question of years. It must be understood against the background of the experience of the individual.
The experience of an individual also seems to have some relevance in the question of language and the question of knowledge. Before getting into that matter, however, I wish to refer back to the time this debate began on May 21 last. Some interventions by members opposite seemed to reflect a concern that under the proposed act British subjects could obtain citizenship after two years of residence. That impression is not supported by the bill. As I understand it, a British subject will have to be here five years just like everyone else.
The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) seemed to be under the impression that time spent in Canada under permit from the Minister of Manpower and Immigration could not be counted toward residence. It can be counted. As the hon. member for Provencher indicated earlier in his opposition to the clause, every day spent in Canada by a person who is not a landed immigrant counts as half a day.
(Mr. Brewin.]
December 8, 1975

Perhaps one might give this example to the hon. member for Provencher to convince him about the merits of this measure. If you have a person here on a minister's permit who is not a landed immigrant, it could be a mother aged 62 who came here as a tourist and who is in the process of being landed-sometimes it takes years-this person may be here for some time before she becomes officially landed. You have also people in other categories. It stands to reason that people in those categories should be given recognition for their residence in Canada. They are here not as landed immigrants, they are here only on a minister's permit, but they are exposed daily to the Canadian environment, to Canadian institutions and they breathe the Canadian air, so whether they are here as landed immigrants or on a minister's permit, surely something can be done to recognize this, in terms of the fact that they are here, if they wish to become Canadian citizens.
I think you can approach this bill from the viewpoint of one who counts hours and days and scrutinizes details, or from the point of view of interpreting Canadian citizenship as, of course, a great gift that is made available to anyone who comes forward and wishes it without really becoming involved in the calculation of half days or full days, or three years or four years. Citizenship is too important to be treated in that way. If it were to be treated in that way it could lead to the dangerous situation we have in some places like Montreal, where there are stagnant pockets of landed immigrants who are very slow in coming forward to request citizenship. This is not good for the country. It is not good for our society if a person who has been here for 10, 15 or 20 years has not, somehow, found the motivation or the channel for coming forward and applying. Something is not quite right there.
Before I am misunderstood, I should like to to stress this point. It is a great characteristic of Canadian citizenship that so far we have resisted the temptation to provide advantages in the law if a person becomes a citizen. In other words, we have kept Canadian citizenship pure, as a thing to be desired if you want to have it: we have not said a person will not be entitled to or will not be qualified for social security measures, or will not have access to certain services and to certain things in society that are desirable. We have resisted that temptation and treated landed immigrants and citizens virtually alike, with very few exceptions. This is why I take exception to the recommendation in the orange paper on immigration which says you would be entitled to sponsor your parents at an earlier age than at present allowed under the law-I believe it is 60-if you have become a Canadian citizen.
I would resent it very deeply if we were to implement that recommendation. A father is a father and a mother is a mother, and the desire on the part of children who are landed immigrants in Canada, who work to raise their children, who pay taxes, should be looked upon on the merits of that very close family relationship, regardless of whether or not the sponsor is a Canadian citizen. I think we have been doing very well over the years in not making such a distinction and we should keep up this fine record.
In this bill there is a provision in relation to knowledge. Perhaps the minister would like to have a look at it before he appears in the committee. In the bill it is said that the
Citizenship
minister will have the power to waive the requirement for knowledge. I would consider that to be a poor practice if it were ever to become an administrative practice. It seems to me that the present way, whereby we require an applicant to memorize answers, to know the names of capitals, to know the name of the Governor General, when it comes to people who are in their fifties or in their sixties who have worked all their lives here, raised their children and sent them to school and done all their duties as citizens, is not reflective of an understanding of what citizenship really means from the viewpoint of the applicant.
It doesn't make sense to encourage people to memorize mechanically certain things. Surely an old lady who came from Europe 55 years ago and comes forward to apply for Canadian citizenship does so for deeply-felt reasons. If she should be judged at all, which I doubt, it should be in the form of a conversation between a judge and herself, a kind of preliminary welcome into the Canadian family, certainly not on the basis of whether she knows certain things which have to be learnt mechanically, which have nothing to do with the maturity of that individual nor with her sense of understanding of the country, because whether or not you know that the capital of Prince Edward Island is a certain city, which for the moment escapes me, has little to do with citizenship.
The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) is prompting me to say that it is Charlottetown. Surely, whether you know the name of the longest river in Canada really has nothing to do with citizenship. But over the years I suppose it was necessary to develop some kind of measurement, particularly when you had a large number of applicants, to determine whether a particular applicant was ready or not. I would much prefer to see a system under which, instead of giving the minister power to waive the requirement for knowledge, which is just a bureaucratic invention, we held classes within a community.
First, we would find out from the viewpoint of the applicants what they would be interested in knowing about Canada. Having established that, and not having decided a priori what is of interest to them but what is of interest to applicants across the country, there would be a fairly uniform pattern. We could then offer courses, and having conducted a certain number of courses for these applicants in a certain way, they would be given a little piece of paper-called whatever you like-and with that piece of paper the applicant would demonstrate to the judge that he or she had taken a certain kind of course. I have in mind a course which would explain the economy of Canada, where our national resources are, where our industries are, what our historical relationship is with other countries, and a few other matters.
I am sure this would be a much more interesting and stimulating experience from the viewpoint of the applicant than having to know the names of capitals or the names of rivers. Therefore, I would say that knowledge of Canadian geography and knowledge of the official languages should not be stressed as a qualification, because we know they are very good citizens in the far north, in the Arctic region, who perhaps do not speak a word of English or French yet they are Canadian citizens. We have Indian people, also, who are not very fluent in either of the two official languages; nevertheless they are fine citizens of our country.

I was glad to learn that we are going to have a new oath of allegiance, to be called the "oath of citizenship", permitting the applicant to identify more with Canada as a country. It would be great if one day we had an oath drafted in simple language, language that everyone can understand with wording less complex and obscure than "fulfil", "heirs" and "allegiance". This would permit applicants to become even more aware of the great step in life they are taking in becoming citizens of Canada. It would give them a deeply felt attachment to and pride in this great country of ours.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) touched briefly on the powers given a citizenship judge to defer applications. My understanding is that a judge does not have these powers under the legislation; the power is given in a regulation that is rather obscurely worded and has been interpreted over the years as being power to defer. As opposed to that, this bill espouses the concept of the power of refusal on the part of the minister for a period of two years, and this will probably remove a certain area of discretionary decision-making on the part of judges. In other words, it is either refusal or not. I should like to defer debate on this subject for clarification to committee, where we can discuss the merits of the former approach and the one contained in the bill. Both need to be examined in greater depth.
Reference was made on the last occasion to the provisions contained in clause 33 and I should like to touch upon this briefly. A few weeks ago a report was tabled in the House by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) under the heading "Federal-Provincial Committee on Foreign Ownership of Land". The report deals with the question of citizenship in relation to land acquisition in Canada. For some time now many of us have been very concerned about foreign interests buying land in Canada, people who are neither Canadian citizens nor landed immigrants. This practice has caused great concern, as already demonstrated by legislation passed in P.E.I. It has also caused real hardship in terms of pushing up the price of land in some of our more densely populated areas, something that in times of inflation particularly commands our attention.
It seems to me that although Canada's territory is vast, we have come to the point where we have to decide whether foreign investors, no matter from which country, should be allowed to invest substantial funds to acquire land in Canada. In the end, this inevitably has the effect of increasing the price of this valuable commodity. The report on land ownership makes a recommendation that I would very much support on this rather delicate question. At page 42 the report is dealing with the acquisition of land and has this to say:
This could be accomplished by an amendment to the Canadian Citizenship Act or some other enactment, providing that aliens could acquire land and interests therein subject to such conditions and terms, including complete prohibition, as might be imposed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council of the province where the land is situated. Such conditions might be made subject to limitations such as the following, e.g., that they may not: restrict on the basis of citizenship acquisitions by bona fide landed immigrants intending to become citizens; conflict with Canada's international legal obligations; discriminate as between aliens on the basis of their different nationalities ... ; hinder foreign states in acquiring property for diplomatic and consular purposes.
If this is a viable route to follow, it seems to me that we will require, either in this bill or in legislation to follow, a measure providing that the acquisition of land in Canada be permitted only in the case of Canadian citizens or landed immigrants. Another question we should ask ourselves is why some people do not take out Canadian citizenship. Surely the reason for this deserves examination. The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) has done extremely good work in recent years by opening up citizenship courts in places removed from the more structured high-rise type of office building in the downtown areas. In other words, he has tried to reach out into the community in offering this specific service.
I suggest we are at the point now where we must go even further. A citizenship judge should become an activist in the community. There are isolated pockets of landed immigrants where people should be Canadian citizens but are not. Judges could let them know where services are available and they could become active participants in the community, particularly in large cities where they could become more visibly involved in the life of the community.
In conclusion, there are other aspects of citizenship with which the bill does not deal. For example, citizenship begins when a person decides to become an immigrant and receives landed immigrant status. After his arrival in Canada, he becomes integrated with the community of his choice, he builds a future for himself and his family over the years, until he or she feels they are ready to take this final step. At the time of taking up citizenship, on that day that person comes out of the minority group to which he or she belongs: sometimes just for the evening, sometimes for the day, sometimes for the duration of the ceremony, sometimes for a month and sometimes even for good. Mostly we find this to be a person who moves comfortably and lives happily at ease in both communities, namely, the major Canadian community as well as the small community from which the citizen has come.
One fact is clear. That to become a Canadian citizen in the lifetime of a person is a conscious act; it is the will of that person, a great experience which reflects a deeply-felt love and attachment for the country. It is for this reason I shall conclude by saying that the measures contained in this legislation should be looked at against the background of the typical applicant who comes forward every day in our courts. He is to be judged accordingly.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak on this bill, which has caused me considerable difficulty. It gives me particular pleasure to follow, in the debate, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). I think many of my colleagues share the feeling I have. It is easy for me to understand the judicial import of this legislation and the techniques and logistics involved, but being Canadian by birth it is impossible for me to share the emotion which I am sure must be felt by the hon. member for Davenport and those for whom Canada is their chosen country. I was very interested in what the hon. member for Davenport had to say and I shall comment on it during my remarks.
I was particularly interested when he said it should be the function of the government to reach out into the

December 8, 1975

community. I believe the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) is calling this his out-reach program. I suggest it has not reached the area I represent and I rather suspect this is the case with respect to the majority of members of this House. I think I part company with the hon. member for Davenport when he says it should be the judiciary which does the work. I am more inclined to think it should be the citizenship branch.
Before coming to grips with the bill itself, may I say I have very grave reservations about the citizenship branch being part of the office of the Secretary of State. It seems to me the citizenship branch is so closely allied with immigration that to put it into two separate ministries makes no sense. I have a great advantage in my riding in having vitally interested and dedicated citizenship officers both in Kitchener and in London. No government officials have given me more co-operation than those two officials. While they have never told me so, I am aware of the difficulty they have through not being with the department with which they have the closest connection and that, obviously, is the Department of Manpower and Immigration. It is beyond me why we continue with this farce of having the citizenship branch under the Secretary of State.
In respect of Bill C-20, I hope later in my remarks to be a little more charitable, but at the outset may I say it is my opinion that this bill has been gathering dust in the citizenship branch for years and all through the twenty-ninth parliament. It is absolutely ridiculous that we are sitting here in the closing days of 1975 debating whether an 18-year old can apply for citizenship. It is absolutely unforgiveable.
Let me relate what has happened in my riding. There are two young men in my riding whose character, education and integrity are beyond question. One wishes to serve his country in the armed forces and the other wishes to serve his country in the RCMP. They were arbitrarily prevented from doing so because their father, for his own good reasons, did not wish to apply for Canadian citizenship. These young men, aged 18 and 19, who wanted to serve their country in the RCMP and the armed forces were arbitrarily excluded from so doing because the Secretary of State sat on this legislation for so long.
When we gave these people the right to vote and to enter into contracts, why did we not give them the right to citizenship? The Secretary of State in the twenty-ninth parliament when we had a minority government could have brought in this legislation to reduce the age to 18 and it would have been passed immediately, but he has sat on it for years. I am not the only one who has introduced a private member's bill to reduce the age. Members of this House from other parties have had similar legislation on the order paper which never has been accepted by the Secretary of State.
The bill received first reading in October, 1974. Seven months later we got around to having the second reading debate. Now, well along in 1975, we are just getting into the third day of debate on this very important piece of legislation. I hope the Secretary of State, as is his habit, will not stand up in this chamber and say that we have to rush this bill through, the way he did in respect of the legislation concerning Reader's Digest and Time magazine. There is no way I will be impressed with the need for haste
Citizenship
in respect of a bill which for three or four years the Secretary of State has not been able to get the cabinet to act on in order to get the legislation before the House.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext: Don't be political.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
I will not be political about this bill. I intend to speak on it and I hope you will stand up and speak on it, too. With one qualification, I agree with the object of this bill as described by the minister. There are three objects. The minister wants a bill that will be equitable, he wants a bill that is logical, and he wants a bill that is liberal. Those were the three hallmarks in the speech he made in Calgary.
There has been one change. The hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Landers), speaking on behalf of the Secretary of State, agreed that it should be equitable and logical but suggested that the word "liberal" should be changed to "consistent". I am delighted. I compliment the Secretary of State and the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster, because to me "liberal" and "consistent" were never synonymous. To achieve these three principles, the minister has rejected the principle of citizenship being a matter of ministerial discretion because-and I quote the minister-this permits the possibility of arbitrary exercise of authority without public or legislative sanction. Therefore, citizenship is to be a right rather than a discretionary act. There is a great deal to be said for this and I can see very great arguments on both sides.
This raises, for me, at least two basic questions. First, why are we always talking about rights rather than responsibilities? It seems to me that in this decade we have had an evasion in respect of coming to grips with responsibility to our fellow citizens and we have become preoccupied with our rights. We are so preoccupied at times that we ignore the fact that every right has a corresponding responsibility. When the minister talks about the right of citizenship, he would encourage me to join forces with him if he spent a little time talking about the responsibilities which flow from that particular right. In all fairness I should say that the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster, in the speech I mentioned earlier, instead of referring to the right of citizenship referred to the qualified right. The hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster is getting closer to the kernel of truth than the minister in his Calgary speech or in his speech in the House.
The second question that this raises is that the bill retains positive ministerial discretion; in other words, the minister can award citizenship but he cannot withhold it. I have to ask this question: If negative ministerial discretion is to be deplored, why is positive ministerial discretion to be acclaimed? To me, this is inconsistent. If there is to be ministerial discretion, why must it only be to award citizenship rather than to withhold it? I hope we will hear from the minister or from a government spokesman in that regard. I would suggest that when this bill goes to committee we should be talking not just about the details of the bill but also about the philosophy behind it, because from reading the minister's speech, not only the one in the House but the one in Calgary, I conclude that he has never

December 8, 1975
Citizenship
come to grips with the philosophical and emotional aspects of this legislation.
I should like to deal for a moment with the part of the bill which deals with British subjects because there is a major change in status there. Frankly, I am not so concerned about the change in status; my major concern has been-I can use no other words to describe it-the absolutely rotten job the government has done in getting information out to British subjects. There were changes some years ago in the Canada Elections Act, which became effective last June 25, under which British subjects were no longer allowed to vote in federal elections. I will not re-fight that battle because that is the law of the country. I raised questions in the House of Commons 2Vi years ago and the minister was courteous enough to send me a letter referring to the campaign to inform British subjects of the change. He wrote;
In the promotion campaign in the media which will accompany these new programs, provisions have been made to draw the attention of British subjects to their electoral rights and their relationship to the Citizenship Act.
I have never heard of this promotional campaign. I read five or six newspapers a day, and I have never seen one word coming from the Secretary of State advising British subjects of their change in status or their change in voting rights. Let me say what I did in my riding. I have quite a number of British subjects, although I have more of German descent. Nevertheless, I had a public forum in my riding in co-operation with the citizenship branch. I repeat, their co-operation was absolutely splendid. We informed these people of their status. I am told that there have been more applications for citizenship from British subjects in my riding than in any other riding in western Ontario. I say that not to take credit for it but simply to indicate that if the Secretary of State had done a proper job probably every riding in Canada would have had a proportionate number of applications for citizenship. The minister has failed miserably in his responsibility in this area.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
This is not just to encourage British subjects or anyone else to apply for citizenship. I do not think we should be salesmen of citizenship. That is something that should come from within, from the heart of the person who has to make that decision. But let me point out that the minister has done nothing to indicate to British subjects that many of them are automatically Canadian citizens. For example, consider the war brides, those who came in the 1940s. Most people do not know that they are Canadian citizens by the operation of the law.
My colleagues may ask, what does it matter so long as they are citizens? It matters when they come to vote or when they apply for a passport. All of us have been faced with the deadline when our passport application has been refused because of lack of proof of citizenship. It certainly matters there. It also matters at the border if you do not have that proof of citizenship. It seems to me that if the Secretary of State intended to honour what I thought was an undertaking in his letter to me of July 17, 1973, he has done a horrible job of it.
My final comment with respect to British subjects is that the new bill makes us citizens of the Commonwealth. I do
|Mr. Jarvis.)
not know what it is, and I am most anxious to find out. I think it would be interesting to hear and I hope that someone on the government side will address himself to that question during the debate.
With respect to the removal of judicial discretion and the right to citizenship, the hon. member for Davenport or the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) welcomed the removal of the criterion that an applicant be of good character. I quote as follows from the minister's Calgary speech where he said the following:
-I think that citizenship judges have interpreted the phrase with responsibility and good sense. But here, as in the case of the discretionary powers of the minister that I discussed earlier, the application of the requirement was necessarily an arbitrary thing. It seemed to us that instead of that nebulous phrase, specific criteria should be set down which could be invoked without fear of abuse.
Under the new bill, certain sections of the Criminal Code and the Narcotics Control Act provide these necessary guidelines. About these guidelines there can be no dispute. After all, a person either has done certain things or he has not; he is certain things or he is not. The removal of the words "good character" is, in our opinion, an important step in the direction away from arbitrary law.
What concerns me is that there has been no indication that I have heard or read in the minister's speech that complaints have been received that citizenship judges have acted arbitrarily. I may be blessed with a rather outstanding one in my riding, covering generally the London area. Frankly, he is a vital person in our community and I welcome his visits to my riding. All hon. members who are served by His Honour Judge Calder welcome him in their ridings. I wonder what has prompted the deletion of these words. I realize they are very general in nature, but what concerns me about the criteria now is the provision that the applicant must have an adequate knowledge of Canada and of the responsibilities and privileges of citizenship.
He may have that knowledge and he also may be the greatest abuser of his rights and responsibilities that ever came before a judge. Yet the judge has no discretion but has to grant him citizenship so long as he has followed the mechanical processes laid down in Bill C-20. The judge is simply following certain criteria. On the other hand, the minister retains discretion to award citizenship. I find this terribly inconsistent. If I had my choice, I would prefer judicial discretion to ministerial discretion. With respect to ministerial discretion, I would like to know the use to which that discretion was put under the old act in exceptional circumstances, and I hope we can get some of that information in committee.
In the new act, where the right to citizenship is emphasized, I notice that the minister is given the right to grant citizenship under a number of clauses, but the minister has the discretion to waive at least two requirements which are rather important. First, the requirement that the applicant has adequate knowledge of one of Canada's official languages; and second, which is perhaps more important, the requirement that the applicant has adequate knowledge of Canada and of the responsibilities and privileges of citizenship. It seems to me that to leave that tremendous power in the minister's hands is dangerous. Finally, the governor in council may order the minister to grant citizenship and the minister shall forthwith grant citizenship to the person named, even though that person has not fulfilled one of the several requirements in the act. So we have a one-way street; we have all this ministerial and
December 8, 1975

governor in council discretion, but we do not have the opposite where the granting of citizenship can be arbitrarily refused.
There has been some difficulty with regard to illegal immigrants. The new legislation says that in order to accumulate his three years of residency an immigrant receives one-half day's credit for every day he was resident in Canada before his lawful admission. I point out to the hon. member for Davenport that that does not mean a person who is here on a student visa or something of that nature. I think the hon. member for Davenport was sidetracked in his speech a few minutes ago in that regard. The oresent legislation says that each full year of residence in Canada by the applicant before his lawful admission is deemed to be a half-year's credit toward his five-year residency requirement.
This raises certain questions which I hope the minister will have an opportunity to answer. First, why the change from years to days as a measurement? Basically, that is what we are doing. I do not believe the minister dealt with this question either in Calgary or last May on second reading. Second, I serve notice on the minister that I will want to know in great detail what use the department has made, under the present legislation, of granting the 50 per cent residency credit for unlawful immigrants. We have never come to grips with that in the chamber, and I for one in committee or at the close of this debate would certainly like a substantial amount of detail as to how that has been applied in the department under the present legislation.
With respect to the five-year rule and the proposed three-year rule, I have checked the history of citizenship legislation which is found in the two-volume work by Mr. Clive Parry, entitled "Nationality and Citizenship Laws of the Commonwealth and Ireland", and I am no clearer now than I was before I checked that unquestioned authority. I go back to the Upper Canada Act, which was the first Canadian statute, and there was an oath of allegiance to be taken within three years. Then it went to seven years, then to five years. Provincial statutes were generally seven years and five years. There was one three-year requirement in British Columbia. The Dominion Act of 1868 repealed provincial legislation, and there was a three-year requirement and after 1880 it became a five-year requirement.
From 1914 to 1946 we were unable to control the law of nationality or naturalization, so we did so by immigration restrictions. The Canadian Citizenship Act of 1946 had a five-year rule and British subjects did not have to go to court. There were amendments in 1967 and 1968. As I say, the history was of no help to me. I hope that in committee we will be able to come to grips with that matter and receive some information from those who know best. I want to hear many witnesses, frankly, from ethnic and other groups. I have heard various opinions from various people, but I am not satisfied.
The period of residency is an arbitrary thing; I realize that. I do not know why we are changing it now. Maybe there is a good reason; I simply have not heard it yet. I hope the committee hearings will give very wide scope to
Citizenship
groups who want to appear, and that we will not have to limit witnesses as we did in the Time-Reader's Digest committee hearings. It is the same committee, but it is a good, hard working committee and we will be willing to listen to people who want to participate in the discussion of this topic. In addition to the five and three-year rule, I want to hear them talk about the philosophy of citizenship, whether it should be a right, a privilege or a discretionary matter.
With regard to equal treatment for men and women, all I can say is that that was recommended five years ago by the royal commission. This is a pretty good indication of the general track record of this department in getting legislation in front of us. I have no quarrel with this legislation in so far as the equality of status between men and women is concerned, but I deplore the length of time it has taken. The old act could have been amended very simply and quickly and I simply cannot understand why that was not done.
I have heard suggestions about retroactivity with regard to citizenship, which the minister has resisted; it is not in the legislation. For example, it has been suggested that children born abroad to Canadian mothers and alien fathers be proclaimed citizens retroactively. My first reaction is to agree with the minister in resisting that type of suggestion, but I want to hear evidence from groups advocating this, because there may be some very good reason of which I or my colleagues are not aware, and perhaps we might be persuaded that this is a more equitable approach to the new citizenship legislation.
In summary, the minister wants legislation which is equitable and logical. He originally wanted legislation that was "liberal," but that is now changed to "consistent" and I applaud that change. With regard to equity, I hope the bill is more equitable than this government has been to 18, 19 and 20-year olds for the last few years, and with regard to equality between men and women. With regard to logic, I have to ask myself whether it is logical to eliminate judicial discretion and replace it with one-way ministerial discretion. Someone will have to do a lot of persuading to convince me that that is more logical. With regard to consistency, I have to ask whether it is consistent to say, on one hand, "You have the right to citizenship", and on the other hand to say, "Even if you fail every single criterion for citizenship, the governor in council may order the granting of citizenship".
I am anxious to discuss these three tests with which the minister has challenged us. Again, I deplore the length of time this legislation has taken and the harsh treatment many of our citizens have received from a complacent Secretary of State. Parts of this legislation should have been introduced at least four or five years ago. There was absolutely no reason for not doing so. I will welcome the legislation in committee and hope it will be given the treatment it deserves, not a ramrodding through, which has been the case with certain other legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the late hour I do not particularly want to use an undue amount of the time of the House, but I should like to make just a couple of points. Like the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), the principal reason I want to speak is that we know the problems in the Citizenship Act. They are closely allied to immigration problems. Having listened to

Citizenship
the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) and the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis), it is quite obvious that they do not understand the problems which promoted the changes in this bill because they do not have large, new Canadian populations in their constituencies.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext: I have 5,000 Germans.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
The hon. member has 5,000 Germans. I do not particularly want to bore the House with a list of the groups I have, because it would take too much time. However, in the urban centres we do know what these problems are and we support this bill wholeheartedly. I do not want to go into the aspects referred to by the hon. member for Greenwood. He made some very good points about the reduction of the age limit from 21 to 18. Also, naturally, all Liberal members would agree that the clause regarding equal status for women and men as to parentage of minor children is quite acceptable in this International Women's Year, as well as being equitable.
I should like to deal with the clause the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot touched upon. There does not seem to be very much disagreement with regard to this clause, which deals with British subjects and requires them to be examined by a citizenship court judge and to take an oath of allegiance. In addition to the large number of new Canadians in my constituency, there are very many old-time residents who have come from the British Isles, and some of their attitudes really baffle me. In the general election many of them surprised me by their reluctance to take out Canadian citizenship. The hon. member for Perth-Wilmot referred to changes in the Canada Elections Act. There seems to be a myth that British people-I was born over there myself-lose some indefinable rights by taking out Canadian citizenship even though they live and work in Canada most of their lives.
Mr. Speaker, I have constituents who arrived here as children at the turn of the century and they still have not taken out citizenship. I agree that this is a deplorable state of affairs. As members of parliament, we must take steps to help these people realize that by taking Canadian citizenship they will not lose any other rights. In fact, I believe that the United Kingdom Citizenship Act of 1949 made provision for all those born in the United Kingdom to retain their rights as citizens of that country. When I was back there working a couple of years ago, I had the same rights as everyone else for health insurance, unemployment insurance and that sort of thing. This is one of the essential points that I should like to bring out.
Members of the official opposition cast aspersions on this party as being againsts the British connection, but many of us were born there and many of us were elected in constituencies where large numbers of the people came from Britain. British citizens should be aware that they are not in danger of losing their rights, but they should realize that Canada and the world have changed since the days of the old empire when British citizens did not have to submit to the same requirements as all other potential citizens. We must wipe out all the inequities in the law, Mr. Speaker, so I am particularly supportive of this aspect of the bill.

I should like now to refer to the three-year requirement for citizenship, although most of the points were covered by my colleague, the hon. member for Davenport. I was surprised at the attitude of the hon. member for Provencher when he spoke of this Canadianization program that he seemed to propose. If you ask applicants in Canadian immigration offices abroad why they want to come to this country, you will find that they know about the rights Canadians have, about free speech and tolerance. It really does not matter how many provincial capitals they know, or how many politicians' names they know. I am sure that even those who do not have a great command of the Englsih language would be able to tell what it means to be a Canadian citizen if they were interviewed in their own language.
The hon. member for Provencher asked why the qualification period should be reduced to three years. I ask why should it not? Surely it would promote a greater interest in and a feeling of belonging to this country. The hon. member for Provencher dealt with clause 5 (1) (b) which provides that for every day during which a person was resident in Canada before his lawful admission for permanent residence, he should be deemed to have accumulated one-half day of residence. He spoke about sanctions for those who have been here illegally. But what about people on minister's permits, for instance? I will not go through all the categories, but there are epileptics, the retarded and even homosexuals. The hon. member criticized this aspect of the bill, yet he was a member of the committee studying the green paper which proposed changes to the immigration law to give these people landed immigrant status. Why should we continue to penalize deserving people because of an anachronism in another law which we all agree should be changed?
These are the points I wanted to make, Mr. Speaker. I want everyone in the House to know that those of us who represent constituencies with large, new Canadian populations wholeheartedly welcome the measures contained in the bill.
